docs.title: Framework
docs.text:
MoeaBench is a framework for multi-objective optimization. The main idea is to provide a flexible tool that allows the user to test the ability of evolutionary algorithms to find redundancy of objectives in benchmark problems. It provides metrics, graphs, and other tools for data analysis.

Benchmark problems

Deb 2005: DTLZ1, DTLZ2, DTLZ3, DTLZ4, DTLZ5, DTLZ6, DTLZ7, DTLZ8, DTLZ9

XinYao-2022: DPF1, DPF2, DPF3, DPF4, DPF5

Algorithms

Many-objective: NSGA-III, U-NSGA-III, SPEA-II, RVEA, MOEAD

docs.title: population
docs.text: The parameter defines the population used by the algorithm, which represents the set of candidate solutions. The population undergoes mutations and crossovers over generations. This process aims to find the best solutions through the evolution of the population.

docs.title: default
docs.text: If not passed as a parameter, the assumed value is 100.

docs.title: generations
docs.text: The parameter defines the number of generations used by the algorithm. Candidate solutions are evaluated at each generation. With each evolution, the algorithm converges toward the set of optimal solutions.

docs.title: default
docs.text: If not passed as a parameter, the assumed value is 300.

docs.title: seed
docs.text:
The parameter defines the value of the random process used by the algorithm:

  • initial population generation
  • selection of the best parents
  • mutations operations
  • crossover operations

docs.title: default
docs.text:
If not passed as a parameter, the assumed value is 1.

docs.title: purpose
docs.text: The GD method calculates the GD of objectives across generations.

docs.title: variables types
docs.text:
The method accepts variables of type experiment.result . For a better understanding of this variable, access the link:

variable experiment.result

docs.title: data format
docs.text:
An array is returned from the method, which can be stored in a variable and manipulated in any way the user prefers:

GD = exp.GD()

docs.title: flexibility
docs.text: The user can assign the following settings

docs.title: generation range
docs.text:
Any generation interval can be chosen. The returned array will be in accordance with this range.

Note: the metric calculation is performed for all objectives within the given range.

GD_gen_130_150 = exp.GD(generations = [130,150])

docs.title: combination objectives
docs.text:
GD calculations can be performed with any combination of objectives.

Note: The metric calculation is based on the objectives selected for all generations.

GD_obj_1_3 = exp.GD(objectives = [1,3])

docs.title: generation range and combination objectives
docs.text:
It is possible to plot with a generation range and a given combination of objectives.

GD_gen_200_210_obj_2_3 = exp.GD(generations = [200,210], objectives = [2,3])

docs.title: default
docs.text:
In default mode, GD is calculated with all objectives and all generations.

GD_all = exp.GD()

docs.title: exceptions
docs.text:
To protect the integrity of the data passed as parameters, certain rules and exceptions are considered. Information regarding exceptions and rules can be accessed at this link:

docs.title: purpose
docs.text: The plot_GD method calculates the GD of objectives across generations and plots the results.

docs.title: variables types
docs.text:
The method accepts variables of type result . For a better understanding of this variable, access the link:

variable experiment.result

docs.title: supported variables
docs.text:
Any number of variables are accepted:

moeabench.plot_GD(exp1.result, exp2.result, exp3.result..)

docs.title: flexibility
docs.text: The user can assign the following settings

docs.title: generation range
docs.text:
Any generation interval can be chosen. The graph will be plotted according to that range:

Note: the metric calculation is performed for all objectives within the given range.

moeabench.plot_GD(exp3.result, exp2.result, exp.result,  generations = [50,200])

docs.title: combination objectives
docs.text:
GD calculations can be performed with any combination of objectives.

Note: The metric calculation is based on the objectives selected for all generations.

moeabench.plot_GD(exp3.result, exp2.result, exp.result,  objectives = [2,3])

docs.title: generation range and combination objectives
docs.text:
It is possible to plot with a generation range and a given combination of objectives.

moeabench.plot_GD(exp3.result, exp2.result, exp.result,  generations = [90,240],  objectives = [1,2])

docs.title: default
docs.text:
In default mode, GD is calculated with all objectives and all generations.

moeabench.plot_GD(exp3.result, exp2.result, exp.result)

docs.text:

self.llist_E_DTLZ = list(E_DTLZ)

    def constraints(self,f,parameter = 1,f_c=[]):
        f_constraints=np.array(f)
        f_c = np.array([np.sum([ f_c**2  for  f_c in f_constraints[linha,0:f_constraints.shape[1]]])-parameter for index,linha in enumerate(range(f_constraints.shape[0]))  ])
        return f_c


    def eval_cons(self,f):
        M_constraints = self.constraints(f)
        eval = M_constraints == 0
        return f[eval]


    def get_Points(self):
        return np.array([*np.random.random((self.get_P(), self.get_N()))*1.0])


    def F1(self,M,th,Gxm):
       theta = list(map(lambda TH: np.cos(TH), th[0:(M-1)]))
       return (1+Gxm)*np.prod(np.column_stack(theta ), axis = 1).reshape(Gxm.shape[0],1)


    def F2(self,M,th,Gxm):
        theta = list(map(lambda TH: np.cos(TH), th[0:(M-2)]))
        return (1+Gxm)*np.prod(np.column_stack(theta ), axis = 1).reshape(Gxm.shape[0],1)*np.column_stack(np.sin(th[(M-2):(M-1)]))


    def F3(self,M,th,Gxm):
        theta = list(map(lambda TH: np.cos(TH), th[0:(M-3)]))
        return (1+Gxm)*np.prod(np.column_stack(theta ), axis = 1).reshape(Gxm.shape[0],1)*np.column_stack(np.sin(th[(M-3):(M-2)]))


    def Fm(self,M,th,Gxm):
        return (1+Gxm)*np.column_stack(np.sin(th[0:1]))


    def get_method(self,enum):
        return self.llist_E_DTLZ[enum]


    def param_F(self):
        dict_F = {
                    self.get_method(0) : self.F1,
                    self.get_method(1) : self.F2,
                    self.get_method(2) : self.F3,
                    self.get_method(3) : self.Fm
                  }
        return dict_F


    def calc_F_M(self,Fi,M):
        if Fi == 1:
            return self.get_method(0)
        elif Fi == 2 and M > 2:
            return self.get_method(1)
        elif Fi >= 3 and Fi <= M-1 and M > 3:
            return self.get_method(2)
        elif Fi == M:
            return self.get_method(3)


    def calc_TH(self,X,Gxm,M):
        return [X[:,Xi:Xi+1]*np.pi/2 if Xi == 0 else (np.pi/(4*(1+Gxm))*(1+2*Gxm*X[:,Xi:Xi+1]))  for Xi in range(0,M-1)]


    def calc_f(self,X,G):
        vet_F_M = [self.calc_F_M(F,self.get_M()) for F, i in enumerate(range(0,self.get_M()), start = 1)]
        return np.column_stack(list(map(lambda Key: self.param_F()[Key](self.get_M(),self.calc_TH(X,G,self.get_M()),G),vet_F_M)))


    def calc_g(self,X):
        return np.sum((X[:,self.get_M()-1:]-0.5)**2, axis = 1).reshape(X.shape[0],1)

The variable D represents the essential objectives of the problem. The evolutionary algorithm must find the essential objectives of the problem and find the Pareto optimal front. The Pareto optimal front is degenerate, characterized by being a POF smaller than M-1 objectives.

docs.title: DPF5
docs.text:
The DPF5 problem has a Pareto optimal front defined by:

\[ \boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_1^2}(X)} + \boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_2^2}(X)} + \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_3^2}(X)} + \boldsymbol{....}}_{\text{M > 3} } + \boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_M^2}(X) = 1} \Longrightarrow \boldsymbol{\sum_{m=1}^M\textcolor{blue}{f_{m}^2} = 1} \]

DPF5 is defined by the following variables:

  • M: Number of objectives in the problem
  • N: Number of decision variables
  • D: Number of essential objectives
  • K: represented by:
\[ \boldsymbol{K}\text{ is the value of the vector } \boldsymbol{\big|X^{\large r}\big|} \text{ where all } \boldsymbol{X_i} \text{ }\boldsymbol{(X_m \in X_n)} \]

The value of N can be obtained by the equation N = D + K - 1.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
The problem is divided into 2 parts:

  • M-D: Where the redundant objectives are located, which may vary according to the size of M and D. It can also change depending on the decision variable x1.
  • M-D+1: Where the essential objectives of the problem are located, with a total of D objectives.

docs.title: Redundancy
docs.text:
Multiobjective benchmark test problems usually have a Pareto front defined by M−1 dimensions, where all objectives are mutually conflicting and independent. The presence of redundant objectives makes the dimension of the Pareto optimal front degenerate, meaning smaller than M−1.

  • M = 10: problem objectives
  • D = 5: essential objectives
  • M-D = 5: redundant objectives

docs.title: DTLZ1
docs.text:
The DTLZ1 problem has a Pareto optimal front formed by a linear hyperplane:

\[ \boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_1}(X)} + \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_2}(X)} + \boldsymbol{....}}_{\text{M > 3} } + \boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_{M-1}}(X)} + \boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_{M}}(X) = 0.5} \Longrightarrow \boldsymbol{\sum_{m=1}^M\textcolor{blue}{f_{M}^*} = 0.5} \]

DTLZ1 is defined by the following variables:

  • M: Number of objectives of the problem
  • N: Number of decision variables
  • K: represented by:
\[ \boldsymbol{K}\text{ is the value of the vector } \boldsymbol{\big|X_M\big|} \text{ where all } \boldsymbol{X_i} \text{ belong to } \boldsymbol{X_M}\text{ }\boldsymbol{(X_i \in X_M)} \]

The value of N can be obtained from the equation N = K+M-1 by substituting the value of K. Alternatively, the value of K can be defined by the equation K = N-M+1, substituting the value of N.

docs.title: For M = 3
docs.text:
\[ \large \underbrace{f_1}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_1}(X)}}, \underbrace{f_2}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_{M-1}}(X)}}, \underbrace{f_3}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_M}(X)}} \]

Where f1 ,f2 and f3 are the objective functions according to the total number of (M = 3).

Define the value of K assuming N = 10, using the equation:

K = 10-3+1 = 8.

Or

Define the value of N assuming K = 8, using the equation:

N = 8+3-1 = 10.

For the problem with M = 3, N = 10 and K = 8, we have:

\[ \large x_1, \underbrace{x_2}_{\boldsymbol{X_{M-1}}}, \underbrace{\underbrace{\underbrace{x_3}_{\boldsymbol{X_M}}, x_4, x_5, x_6, x_7, x_8, x_9, x_{10}}_{\boldsymbol{K = \big|X_M\big| = (X_I \in X_M)}}}_{\textcolor{darkred}{\Large \boldsymbol{g(X_M)}}} \]

The positions XM-1 and XM are represented by x2 and x3, respectively. The vector size | XM | is defined by K = 8, starting at x3 and continuing until the last K = 8 variables, denoted by x10.

The function g( XM ) corresponds to the decision variables within the range of | XM | (x3 x4 x5 x6 x7 x8 x9 x10), and must be minimized by evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs). When this function reaches g = 0, the Pareto optimal front of the problem is found.

docs.title: For M = 4
docs.text:
\[ \large \underbrace{f_1}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_1}(X)}}, \underbrace{f_2}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_2}(X)}}, \underbrace{f_3}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_{M-1}}(X)}}, \underbrace{f_4}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_M}(X)}} \]

Where f1, f2, f3, and f4 are the objective functions according to the total number of (M = 4).

Define the value of K assuming N = 10, using the equation:

K = 10-4+1 = 7.

Or

Define the value of N assuming K = 7, using the equation:

N = 7+4-1 = 10.

For the problem with M = 4, N = 10 and K = 7, we have:

\[ \large x_1, x_2, \underbrace{x_3}_{\boldsymbol{X_{M-1}}}, \underbrace{\underbrace{\underbrace{x_4}_{\boldsymbol{X_M}}, x_5, x_6, x_7, x_8, x_9, x_{10}}_{\boldsymbol{K = \big|X_M\big| = (X_I \in X_M)}}}_{\textcolor{darkred}{\Large \boldsymbol{g(X_M)}}} \]

The positions XM-1 and XM are represented by x3 and x4, respectively. The vector size | XM | is defined by K = 7, starting at x4 and continuing until the last K = 7 variables, denoted by x10.

The function g( XM ) corresponds to the decision variables within the range of | XM | (x4 x5 x6 x7 x8 x9 x10), and must be minimized by evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs). When this function reaches g = 0, the Pareto optimal front of the problem is found.

docs.title: Function g
docs.text:
The purpose of the function g( XM ) is to maximize the distance from the POF of the problem, attracting the evolutionary algorithms to local Pareto fronts.

When the vector | XM | reaches the values | 0.5 0.5 .... 0.5 |, the true POF of the problem is obtained.

\[ \textcolor{darkred}{\boldsymbol{g(X_M)} = 100 \bigg[\big|X_m\big|+\displaystyle\sum_{X_I \in X_M} (x_i-0.5)^2-\cos(20\pi(x_i-0.5))\bigg]} \]

docs.title: Objective functions
docs.text:
Each objective function receives a value from the function g( XM ). The POF of the problem is directly linked to g( XM ).

\[ \textcolor{blue}{f_1}(X)=\frac{1}{2}x_1 x_2...x_{M-1}(1+\boldsymbol{\textcolor{darkred}{g(X_M)}}), \] \[ \textcolor{blue}{f_2}(X)=\frac{1}{2}x_1 x_2...(1-x_{m-1})(1+\boldsymbol{\textcolor{darkred}{g(X_M)}}), \] \[ \textcolor{blue}{f_{M-1}}(X)=\frac{1}{2}x_1 (1-x_2)(1+\boldsymbol{\textcolor{darkred}{g(X_M)}}), \] \[ \textcolor{blue}{f_M}(X)=\frac{1}{2}(1-x_1)(1+\boldsymbol{\textcolor{darkred}{g(X_M)}}) \] ←

docs.title: DTLZ2
docs.text:
The DTLZ2 problem has a Pareto optimal front shaped as a hypersphere:

\[ \boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_1^2}(X)} + \boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_2^2}(X)} + \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_3^2}(X)} + \boldsymbol{....}}_{\text{M > 3}} + \boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_M^2}(X) = 1} \Longrightarrow \boldsymbol{\sum_{m=1}^M\textcolor{blue}{f_{M}^2} = 1} \]

DTLZ2 is defined by the following variables:

  • M: Number of objectives of the problem
  • N: Number of decision variables
  • K: Represented by:
\[ \boldsymbol{K}\text{ is the value of the vector } \boldsymbol{\big|X_M\big|} \text{ where all } \boldsymbol{X_i} \text{ belong to } \boldsymbol{X_M}\text{ }\boldsymbol{(X_i \in X_M)} \]

The value of N can be obtained using the equation N = K + M - 1, replacing the value of K. Alternatively, K can be defined using K = N - M + 1, replacing the value of N.

docs.title: For M = 3
docs.text:
\[ \large \underbrace{f_1}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_1}(X)}}, \underbrace{f_2}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_{2}}(X)}}, \underbrace{f_3}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_M}(X)}} \]

Where f1, f2, and f3 are the objective functions according to the total number of objectives (M = 3).

Define the value of K assuming N = 10, using the equation:

K = 10 − 3 + 1 = 8.

Or

Define the value of N assuming K = 8, using the equation:

N = 8 + 3 − 1 = 10.

For the problem with M = 3, N = 10, and K = 8, we have:

\[ \large x_1, \underbrace{x_2}_{\boldsymbol{X_{M-1}}}, \underbrace{\underbrace{\underbrace{x_3}_{\boldsymbol{X_M}}, x_4, x_5, x_6, x_7, x_8, x_9, x_{10}}_{\boldsymbol{K = \big|X_M\big| = (X_I \in X_M)}}}_{\textcolor{darkred}{\Large \boldsymbol{g(X_M)}}} \]

The positions XM−1 and XM correspond to x2 and x3, respectively. The vector size |XM| is defined by K = 8, starting from x3 and continuing through the last variable x10.

The function g(XM) corresponds to the decision variables within the range |XM| (x3 x4 x5 x6 x7 x8 x9 x10) and must be minimized by the evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs). When g = 0, the Pareto optimal front of the problem is found.

docs.title: For M = 4
docs.text:
\[ \large \underbrace{f_1}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_1}(X)}}, \underbrace{f_2}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_2}(X)}}, \underbrace{f_3}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_{3}}(X)}}, \underbrace{f_4}_{\boldsymbol{\textcolor{blue}{f_M}(X)}} \]

Where f1, f2, f3, and f4 are the objective functions according to the total number of objectives (M = 4).

Define the value of K assuming N = 10, using the equation:

K = 10 − 4 + 1 = 7.

Or

Define the value of N assuming K = 7, using the equation:

N = 7 + 4 − 1 = 10.

For the problem with M = 4, N = 10, and K = 7, we have:

\[ \large x_1, x_2, \underbrace{x_3}_{\boldsymbol{X_{M-1}}}, \underbrace{\underbrace{\underbrace{x_4}_{\boldsymbol{X_M}}, x_5, x_6, x_7, x_8, x_9, x_{10}}_{\boldsymbol{K = \big|X_M\big| = (X_I \in X_M)}}}_{\textcolor{darkred}{\Large \boldsymbol{g(X_M)}}} \]

The positions XM−1 and XM correspond to x3 and x4, respectively. The vector size |XM| is defined by K = 7, starting from x4 and continuing through x10.

The function g(XM) corresponds to the decision variables within the range |XM| (x4 x5 x6 x7 x8 x9 x10) and must be minimized by the evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs). When g = 0, the Pareto optimal front of the problem is reached.

docs.title: g function
docs.text:
The purpose of the function g(XM) is to maximize the distance from the Pareto optimal front (POF) of the problem, attracting the evolutionary algorithms toward local Pareto fronts.

When the vector |XM| reaches the values |0.5 0.5 .... 0.5|, the POF of the problem is found.

\[ \textcolor{darkred}{\boldsymbol{g(X_M)} = \sum_{X_I\in X_M} (x_i - 0.5)^2} \]

docs.title: Objective functions
docs.text:
Each objective function receives a value from the function g(XM). The Pareto optimal front (POF) of the problem is directly linked to g(XM).

\[ \textcolor{blue}{f_1}(X)=(1+\boldsymbol{\textcolor{darkred}{g(X_M)}})\text{ }cos(x_1\pi/2)\text{...} cos(x_{M-2}\pi/2)\text{ } cos(x_{M-1}\pi/2), \] \[ \textcolor{blue}{f_2}(X)=(1+\boldsymbol{\textcolor{darkred}{g(X_M)}})\text{ }cos(x_1\pi/2)\text{...} cos(x_{M-2}\pi/2)\text{ } sin(x_{M-1}\pi/2), \] \[ \textcolor{blue}{f_3}(X)=(1+\boldsymbol{\textcolor{darkred}{g(X_M)}})\text{ }cos(x_1\pi/2)\text{...} sin(x_{M-2}\pi/2), \] \[ \textcolor{blue}{f_4}(X)=(1+\boldsymbol{\textcolor{darkred}{g(X_M)}})\text{ }sin(x_1\pi/2) \] ←

docs.title: Method
docs.text: The method POFsamples intentionally modifies the vector | XM | to the values | 0.0 0.0 .... 0.0 |, making the function value g( XM ) = 0. The purpose is to make the Pareto optimal front of the problem visible.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
The values of the decision variables are randomly generated while respecting the following condition: 0 ≤ xi ≤ 1 for i = 1, 2 ... N.

docs.title: DTLZ8
docs.text:
The DTLZ8 problem has a Pareto optimal front formed by a straight line and a linear hyperplane.

DTLZ8 is defined by the following variables:

  • M: Number of objectives of the problem
  • N: Number of decision variables, represented by: 10M

docs.title: Method
docs.text: The dtlz8.POFsamples() method creates a matrix [ gj(x) , gM(x) ] with the same number of points/solutions as [ M ]. Each point of the [ M ] matrix is validated according to the equivalent solution [ gj(x) , gM(x) ] ≥ 0. The generated Pareto optimal front is an arithmetic constraint for the problem and does not directly produce the POF. But it provides the set of necessary constraints for evolutionary algorithms to search for all possible solution sets through the evolution of generations, population and mutation.
